profile.name: Hiplet
profile.tagline: Pointe technique reimagined through urban rhythm and African dance roots.
profile.insight: Created by Homer Hans Bryant in Chicago, Hiplet fuses traditional pointe work with hip-hop and African dance, reaching viral fame in May 2016 when Instagram videos of young CMDC dancers went global.
profile.profile: Hiplet is a contemporary dance style originating from the Chicago Multi-Cultural Dance Center (CMDC) under the direction of Homer Hans Bryant. Fusing classical ballet pointe technique with hip-hop, African dance roots, and urban pop music, the genre provides young dancers of color a platform to express their contemporary cultural identity within classical forms. Dancers perform traditional ballet footwork and pointe exercises modified with sharper angles, off-center balances, and fluid torso movement. The style gained global visibility in May 2016 through social media, leading to national television broadcasts and mainstream performances. The CMDC remains the primary center dedicated to training dancers in Hiplet.
profile.profile_long:
### Origins and History
Hiplet is a dance style created by Homer Hans Bryant at the Chicago Multi-Cultural Dance Center (CMDC). Its origins trace back to Bryant's earlier fusion experiments, notably his 1992 work "Rap Ballet" (also referenced as originating in 1994). The term "Hiplet" was explicitly coined in 2009 to describe this specific integration of classical ballet pointe technique and hip-hop movement. The style builds on a broader historical continuum of artists attempting to bridge classical Eurocentric ballet with urban dance forms rooted in African traditions, breaking past long-standing racialized and gendered barriers in classical dance.

In May 2016, Hiplet achieved widespread public attention after videos of CMDC dancers performing the style went viral on Instagram, gathering thousands of views worldwide. This digital exposure led to invitations for television broadcasts, including performances on ABC News and *Good Morning America*, as well as presentations on TEDx platforms. The rapid dissemination via digital media highlighted the role of social archives and online platforms in introducing contemporary dance innovations to global audiences.

### How It Is Danced
Ballet serves as the technical core of Hiplet. Dancers require years of formal ballet training to build the ankle strength and alignment necessary to perform safely on pointe. Rather than strictly adhering to traditional classical ballet's vertical posture and turn-out, Hiplet incorporates sharper angles, off-center isolations, and relaxed, fluid torso dynamics drawn from hip-hop and African dance traditions. 

Execution involves rising to full pointe while executing hip-hop grooving, rhythmic foot taps, lower body dips, and sharp directional accents. Dancers must maintain classical control and balance while breaking away from classical alignment, demanding rigorous core stability to prevent injury during sudden rhythm changes and non-traditional weight transfers.

### Music and Instruments
Unlike traditional ballet, which is accompanied by classical orchestral scores, Hiplet is choreographed to urban music, hip-hop tracks, and contemporary pop beats. The musical rhythm features heavy basslines, syncopated drum patterns, and sharp accents. The choreography directly interacts with these urban musical meters, using the hard box of the pointe shoe to strike rhythmic accents against the floor.

### Costume and Setting
Performance attire in Hiplet retains traditional ballet elements while adapting to the identity of its dancers. Performers typically wear traditional ballet leotards, tights, and buns. Crucially, dancers of color frequently dye their pointe shoes and tights to match their natural skin tones, challenging the historical standard of pink ballet apparel and emphasizing cultural representation. Hiplet is trained within studio environments like the CMDC and performed on theatrical stages, television sets, and digital video formats.

### Occasions and Meaning
Hiplet provides young, predominantly Black dancers and dancers of color—typically between the ages of 12 and 16 during initial training—an avenue for self-expression and cultural representation within a discipline that has historically excluded them. By blending ballet with urban cultural heritage, the style offers a contemporary art form that reflects the lived experiences of its performers, redefining who can participate in high-level pointe work and expanding the aesthetic boundaries of classical dance.

sections.origins_and_history: Created by Homer Hans Bryant at the Chicago Multi-Cultural Dance Center (CMDC), Hiplet traces back to Bryant's 1992 "Rap Ballet" (also cited as 1994). The term "Hiplet" was coined in 2009. The style gained international prominence in May 2016 through viral Instagram videos, leading to appearances on ABC News, Good Morning America, and TEDx.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Hiplet pairs rigorous ballet pointe technique with hip-hop and African dance movement. Dancers employ traditional pointe shoes to perform sharp angles, off-balance shifts, and fluid torso dynamics. Solid classical technique developed over years of practice is required to execute the style safely.
sections.music_and_instruments: Hiplet replaces classical orchestral music with urban music, hip-hop, and pop tracks. The movement accents syncopated rhythms, heavy basslines, and modern musical beats.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear traditional ballet attire, including leotards, tights, and hair buns. A defining element is that dancers of color dye their tights and pointe shoes to match their skin tones. Settings range from dance studios and television studios to public stages and digital video platforms.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Hiplet serves as a contemporary vehicle for dancers of color—predominantly young Black dancers between 12 and 16 years old—to engage with pointe work while expressing their urban culture and personal identity within a field that historically lacked diversity.
sections.notable_figures: Homer Hans Bryant is the founder of the Chicago Multi-Cultural Dance Center and creator of Hiplet. Professional ballet dancer Misty Copeland is also associated with Bryant's advocacy for Black dancers in classical ballet.
sections.lineage: Evolved from classical ballet and hip-hop/African dance fusions, drawing a direct lineage from Homer Hans Bryant's 1992/1994 "Rap Ballet" to the formal coining of Hiplet in 2009 at the Chicago Multi-Cultural Dance Center.

movement_profile.posture: Blends vertical classical ballet posture with off-center alignment and relaxed torso flexibility
movement_profile.footwork: Ballet en pointe work combined with sharp urban foot shifts and syncopated floor contact
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Classical ballet arm lines (port de bras) punctuated by sharp angles and hip-hop movement isolations
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Fluid, isolated hip and torso movements rooted in African dance and urban hip-hop
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Flexible, including studio formations, ensemble stage arrangements, and camera-facing broadcast framing
movement_profile.partnering: Primarily solo or synchronized group alignment

signature_moves.name: Pointe hip isolation
signature_moves.description: Isolating hip movements while standing en pointe.

signature_moves.name: Off-center relevé
signature_moves.description: Rising en pointe while shifting the spine and upper body away from traditional vertical alignment.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Floor-level pointe work, relevés, and occasional dynamic bounds
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Attempting Hiplet en pointe without years of prior ballet technical preparation and ankle conditioning.

connections.name: Ballet

connections.note: Provides the rhythmic structure, hip/torso isolations, and sharp movement angles.

seniors.seated_version: Perform hip-hop arm isolations and seated foot ankle-points to syncopated rhythms while fully supported.
seniors.standing_version: Perform soft ankle relevés at the barre or near a chair, omitting full pointe work while integrating gentle torso isolations.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Slower tempo with reduced range of motion in hips and ankles.

children.game_version: Rhythmic freeze-dance game matching hip-hop arm angles and flat-foot relevés to musical beats.
children.counts: Basic 4/4 counts with emphasis on clear rhythmic downbeats.
avoid: Pointe shoes without years of prior technical ballet training
